rows.definition: The amount of radiation energy deposited in matter per unit mass, measured in gray (Gy) — where 1 Gy equals 1 joule of energy absorbed by 1 kilogram of material. It applies to any absorbing material, but in health physics it usually describes energy absorbed by body tissue. It differs from equivalent dose (measured in sieverts), which weights each radiation type by its biological effect.
quick_facts: 1 Gy = 1 joule of energy per kilogram
Applies to any material, not just living tissue
Different from equivalent dose, which is measured in sieverts
A short whole-body dose of ~5 Gy is often fatal without medical care
Measured with dosimeters and ionization chambers
rows.debunking_snippet: Absorbed dose alone doesn't tell you the biological risk. A gray of alpha radiation causes far more tissue damage than a gray of X-rays — that's why equivalent dose (sieverts) exists.

rows.definition: Acute radiation syndrome is the illness caused by a very high radiation exposure delivered over a short period of time. The dose threshold is about 1 sievert (1000 millisieverts). It can cause symptoms such as nausea and vomiting within hours. The everyday doses people receive are far below it.
quick_facts: Needs a very large dose in a short time
The threshold is about 1 sievert, or 1000 millisieverts
Symptoms such as nausea and vomiting can start within hours
rows.debunking_snippet: “Any radiation exposure leads to radiation sickness.” Exposure to the low levels of radiation in the environment does not cause immediate health effects. Acute radiation syndrome needs about 1000 millisieverts in a short time.

rows.definition: A kind of radioactive decay in which a nucleus gives off an alpha particle: 2 protons and 2 neutrons stuck together, the nucleus of a helium atom. The nucleus that is left has 2 fewer protons and 2 fewer neutrons, so it is a different element. Alpha decay is common in very heavy nuclei such as uranium.
quick_facts: An alpha particle is 2 protons and 2 neutrons
It is the nucleus of a helium atom
The daughter has 2 fewer protons, so it is a different element
It is common in very heavy nuclei
Alpha is a particle, not electromagnetic radiation

rows.definition: A heavy, positively charged particle made of 2 protons and 2 neutrons — identical to a helium-4 nucleus — emitted by heavy, unstable nuclei such as uranium, radium, and radon during alpha decay. Alpha particles barely penetrate matter: paper or the outer layer of skin stops them. But they ionize intensely along their short path, making them among the most damaging radiations when alpha emitters are inhaled or ingested.
quick_facts: Identical to a helium-4 nucleus: 2 protons + 2 neutrons
Stopped by a sheet of paper, skin, or a few centimeters of air
Cause dense ionization along their very short path
Most dangerous when inhaled or swallowed — e.g. radon gas in lungs
Emitted by heavy elements like uranium, radium, and radon
rows.debunking_snippet: “Alpha radiation is harmless because it can't get through skin.” Outside the body, mostly true — but one alpha particle inside the lungs tears through countless cells. That's why inhaled radon is a leading cause of lung cancer among non-smokers.

rows.definition: American nuclear physicist (1915–2006) who co-invented the pressurized water reactor — the design used today in most naval vessels and about two-thirds of the world's power reactors — and later championed molten salt reactors at Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), leading its Molten Salt Reactor Experiment. He directed ORNL from 1955 to 1973 and became an early advocate of nuclear safety culture, arguing reactors should be inherently safe, not just engineered to be safe. He was dismissed in 1973 after clashing with Washington over reactor priorities.
quick_facts: Co-invented the pressurized water reactor (PWR)
Led ORNL's Molten Salt Reactor Experiment (first criticality 1965)
Directed Oak Ridge National Laboratory, 1955–1973
Advocated 'inherent safety' long before it was industry standard
Dismissed in 1973 after opposing the fast-breeder program

rows.definition: Soviet theoretical physicist (1921–1989), often called the father of the Soviet hydrogen bomb (first tested 1953). Horrified by the arms race he helped accelerate, he became the USSR's most prominent dissident, campaigning against nuclear testing and for human rights. He won the 1975 Nobel Peace Prize and was exiled to the closed city of Gorky from 1980 to 1986; the European Parliament's Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought is named in his honor.
quick_facts: Key designer of the Soviet hydrogen bomb (tested 1953)
Awarded the 1975 Nobel Peace Prize
Exiled to Gorky (1980–1986) for his dissent
The EU's Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought honors him
His ideas influenced Gorbachev's reforms of the late 1980s

rows.definition: American physicist (1892–1962) who discovered the Compton effect in 1923: X-rays scattering off electrons transfer energy like colliding particles, proving that light behaves as particles (photons) as well as waves. He shared the 1927 Nobel Prize in Physics. During World War II he directed the Manhattan Project's Metallurgical Laboratory at the University of Chicago, where Enrico Fermi's team achieved Chicago Pile-1, the world's first self-sustaining chain reaction.
quick_facts: Discovered the Compton effect (1923)
Shared the 1927 Nobel Prize in Physics with C.T.R. Wilson
Directed the Met Lab, Chicago (1942–1945)
Oversaw Chicago Pile-1 — the first controlled chain reaction
Later chancellor of Washington University (1945–1953)

rows.definition: The smallest unit of ordinary matter that keeps the identity of a chemical element. Every atom has a tiny, dense nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons bound to it electromagnetically. Atoms are overwhelmingly empty space — nearly all the mass sits in the nucleus, yet the electron cloud spans roughly 100,000 times farther out.
quick_facts: Building block of all ordinary matter
Over 99.9% of an atom's mass is packed into its nucleus
Electrons occupy probability clouds (orbitals), not fixed orbits
About 10 million atoms lined up span just 1 millimeter
Number of protons fixes which element it is
rows.debunking_snippet: “Atoms are tiny solid balls.” They're almost entirely empty space — the solid feel of matter comes from electromagnetic forces between electron clouds, not hard surfaces actually touching.

rows.definition: The number of protons in an atom's nucleus, symbolized Z. It uniquely defines a chemical element — every carbon atom has Z = 6, every uranium atom Z = 92 — and fixes the element's place in the periodic table. In a neutral atom it also equals the number of orbiting electrons, which is what governs chemistry.
quick_facts: Symbol: Z
Defines an atom's chemical element — unique per element
Equals proton count (and electron count when neutral)
Carbon: Z = 6 · Uranium: Z = 92
Changing Z requires a nuclear reaction — this is transmutation

rows.definition: The ionizing radiation present in the environment at all times: cosmic rays from space, radon gas seeping from soil and rock, naturally radioactive materials in the ground, food, and even our own bodies (potassium-40 and carbon-14), plus a small man-made share such as medical procedures and fallout. It varies widely by location — altitude increases the cosmic share, while some regions have uranium-rich soils.
quick_facts: Everyone on Earth is exposed to it constantly
≈2.4 mSv per year worldwide from natural sources (UNSCEAR)
Radon gas is the largest single natural contributor
Flying raises your dose — more cosmic rays at altitude
Varies strongly by location, altitude, and local geology

sources.title: Sources and Effects of Ionizing Radiation

rows.debunking_snippet: “All radiation is man-made.” Natural background accounts for the majority of human exposure — life evolved with it.

rows.definition: The SI unit of radioactivity: one nuclear decay per second, named after French physicist Henri Becquerel, who discovered radioactivity in 1896. Because individual decays are rare events for large samples, real-world activities are often huge numbers — household smoke detectors hold about 30,000 Bq of americium-241. The older unit, the curie (Ci), equals 3.7×10¹⁰ Bq.
quick_facts: 1 Bq = exactly one nuclear decay per second
Named after Henri Becquerel, discoverer of radioactivity (1896)
Activity tells you how many decays occur — not how much energy or danger
1 curie (Ci) = 37 billion Bq
Smoke detectors contain ~30 kBq americium-241
rows.debunking_snippet: “High activity means high danger.” Not necessarily — becquerels count decays, but dose depends on energy, radiation type, distance, and whether the source gets inside your body.

rows.definition: A kind of radioactive decay in which a nucleus gives off a beta particle, a fast electron. In the usual kind, beta-minus decay, a neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton and an electron is emitted, along with a tiny particle called an antineutrino. The number of protons goes up by one, so the nucleus becomes a different element.
quick_facts: A beta particle is a fast electron
A neutron changes into a proton and an electron is emitted
The electron was not orbiting the nucleus before
A tiny antineutrino comes out too
The number of protons goes up by one, so the element changes
rows.debunking_snippet: “The beta electron was one of the atom's orbiting electrons.” It is made in the decay itself, when a neutron changes into a proton.

rows.definition: A high-speed electron (β⁻) or positron (β⁺) thrown out of an unstable nucleus during beta decay — effectively a neutron converting into a proton (or vice versa) inside the nucleus. Beta particles are far more penetrating than alphas: they can slip through skin and paper but stop in a few millimeters of plastic or aluminum. Positron-emitting isotopes like carbon-11 and fluorine-18 power PET medical scans.
quick_facts: An electron (β⁻) or positron (β⁺) from the nucleus
Stopped by a few mm of plastic or aluminum
Can penetrate slightly beyond dead skin layers
Positron emitters enable PET medical imaging
Emitted across the whole periodic table — e.g. carbon-14, tritium
rows.debunking_snippet: “Any metal shield makes beta radiation harmless.” Dense metals like lead can actually make things worse — betas striking them emit secondary X-rays (bremsstrahlung). Low-density plastic or acrylic is the right shield.

rows.definition: The energy needed to pull a nucleus apart into its separate protons and neutrons — equivalently, the energy released when those nucleons bind together. It comes from the mass converted to energy described by E = mc²: a bound nucleus weighs less than the sum of its parts (the mass defect). Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56 (with nickel-62 holding the precise record), which is why energy is released by splitting heavy nuclei (fission) and fusing light ones (fusion) — both move toward the iron peak.
quick_facts: Energy required to disassemble a nucleus completely
Explained by mass defect via E = mc²
Nickel-62 holds the record binding energy per nucleon; iron-56 is the classic reference
Fission and fusion both release energy by moving toward the iron peak
Determines which nuclei are stable vs. radioactive

rows.definition: A self-sustaining series of nuclear fission events: each fission splits a heavy nucleus and releases 2–3 fresh neutrons, which can go on to split further nuclei. If exactly one fission per generation goes on to cause another (k = 1), the chain is critical and steady — that's a reactor. More than one (k > 1) grows exponentially — that's a bomb or a supercritical accident. Reactors stay controllable thanks to delayed neutrons, which act as a slow-moving fraction of the chain.
quick_facts: Each fission releases 2–3 neutrons
Critical (k = 1): steady power · supercritical: exponential growth
Delayed neutrons give reactors their controllability
Control rods tune the chain by absorbing neutrons
Requires enough fissile material and the right neutron energy
rows.debunking_snippet: “A reactor can explode like an atomic bomb.” It can't — reactor fuel is far too dilute in fissile material (a few % U-235 vs >90% for weapons). Chernobyl's explosion was steam and chemical energy, never a nuclear blast.

rows.definition: Chinese-American experimental physicist (1912–1997), called the 'First Lady of Physics'. During the Manhattan Project she improved gaseous-diffusion uranium enrichment. Her crowning achievement came in 1956: the Wu experiment confirmed that mirror symmetry (parity) is violated in beta decay — a discovery so fundamental it won Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen-Ning Yang the 1957 Nobel Prize while Wu herself was overlooked.
quick_facts: Ran the decisive 1956 parity-violation experiment
Lee & Yang won the Nobel; many argue Wu deserved it too
Improved gaseous-diffusion uranium enrichment (Manhattan Project)
Nicknamed the 'First Lady of Physics'
Awarded the inaugural Wolf Prize in Physics (1978)

rows.definition: The massive reinforced-concrete dome or box — typically about a meter thick with a steel liner — that encloses a reactor's primary system. It is the final barrier in the defense-in-depth strategy: built to hold steam pressure from a loss-of-coolant accident, withstand earthquakes and external impacts, and keep radioactive material sealed inside even during severe core damage. Containment did its job at Three Mile Island (1979); at Fukushima (2011) it largely contained the meltdowns despite hydrogen explosions damaging the buildings.
quick_facts: Final barrier between the reactor and the public
Reinforced concrete ~1 m thick with a steel liner
Designed against quakes, impacts, and internal pressure
Held firm at Three Mile Island (1979)
One layer of the defense-in-depth strategy

rows.definition: Neutron-absorbing rods — boron carbide, cadmium, silver-indium-cadmium, or hafnium — moved in and out of a reactor core to regulate the chain reaction. Inserted deeper, they soak up more neutrons and power falls; withdrawn, power rises. On an emergency shutdown (scram) they slam fully in within seconds, stopping the fission chain. Because they rely on gravity or hydraulics rather than electronics, they fail safe.
quick_facts: Made of neutron absorbers: boron, cadmium, hafnium
Inserted deeper → less power; withdrawn → more power
SCRAM: full insertion in seconds stops the chain reaction
Designed to fail safe — gravity drops them on power loss
Absorb neutrons without themselves becoming dangerously unstable
rows.debunking_snippet: “Turning off a reactor is like switching off a light.” Control rods stop the fission chain almost instantly — but radioactive decay heat keeps the fuel hot for days, which is why cooling continues long after shutdown.

rows.definition: High-energy particles — mostly protons and atomic nuclei — arriving from outside the solar system (galactic cosmic rays, born in supernovae) plus bursts of solar particles from the Sun. When they smash into the atmosphere they trigger showers of secondary particles; those secondaries, not the originals, account for nearly all cosmic dose at ground level. Exposure roughly doubles every 2,000 meters of altitude, which is why airline crews receive among the highest occupational doses of any profession.
quick_facts: Origins: supernovae across the galaxy, plus solar storms
At ground level we're hit mainly by secondary shower particles
Dose roughly doubles every 2 km of altitude
Airline crews get the highest occupational doses in civilian work
Earth's atmosphere and magnetic field are our shields
rows.debunking_snippet: “Cosmic radiation is just sunlight.” It isn't light at all — it's charged particles, mostly from far beyond the solar system, moving at nearly light speed.

rows.definition: The smallest amount of fissile material that can sustain a chain reaction, given a particular shape, density, purity, and surroundings. A bare sphere needs about 52 kg of weapons-grade uranium-235 or about 10 kg of plutonium-239; surrounding the core with a reflector that bounces neutrons back can cut those figures dramatically. Squeeze a subcritical mass into a supercritical one fast enough — by implosion or gun assembly — and you have a weapon; arrange it just right in a lattice and you have a steady reactor.
quick_facts: Bare sphere: ≈52 kg U-235, ≈10 kg Pu-239
Depends on shape, purity, density, and neutron reflection
A tamper/reflector can cut the required mass several-fold
Weapons achieve supercriticality via implosion or gun assembly
Reactors arrange fuel to run exactly critical, no more

rows.definition: A compact circular particle accelerator invented by Ernest O. Lawrence in 1930. Electric fields kick charged particles faster with each pass while a magnetic field bends them into a widening spiral until they exit at high energy. Cyclotrons are workhorses of nuclear medicine: hospital-based machines bombard targets to make short-lived positron emitters such as fluorine-18 for PET scans. (Technetium-99m, the most-used diagnostic isotope, comes mainly from reactors instead.) Lawrence won the 1939 Nobel Prize in Physics for the cyclotron.
quick_facts: Invented by Ernest O. Lawrence (1930)
Accelerates particles in a spiral using electric + magnetic fields
Makes PET isotopes like fluorine-18 in hospitals
Compact next to kilometer-long linear accelerators
Lawrence won the 1939 Nobel Prize for it

rows.definition: The nucleus that is left after a radioactive decay. It is a different nucleus from the parent. The daughter can be stable, and then the changing stops, or it can be unstable too, and then it decays again. A run of decays like this is a decay chain.
quick_facts: The daughter is the nucleus the parent becomes
It is a different nucleus, so nothing simply vanishes
It can be stable or unstable
An unstable daughter decays again
A chain ends at a stable daughter
rows.debunking_snippet: “Every decay makes a stable atom.” The daughter can be unstable too, and then it decays again.

rows.definition: The spontaneous transformation of an unstable nucleus into a more stable configuration by emitting radiation — an alpha particle, beta electron or positron, gamma ray, or occasionally a whole neutron or split. Quantum mechanics makes each atom's timing unknowable yet the crowd's behavior perfectly predictable: exponential halving governed by half-life. Decay chains can run many steps — uranium-238 takes 14 transformations over billions of years before settling as stable lead-206.
quick_facts: Random per atom, precisely predictable per sample
Main modes: alpha, beta (β⁻/β⁺), gamma, spontaneous fission
U-238 chain: 14 decays over 4.5 billion years → lead-206
Nothing humans do speeds it up meaningfully
Each step changes the element — transmutation in action
rows.debunking_snippet: “We could neutralize waste if we heated or zapped it.” Decay rates are set inside the nucleus and shrug off temperature, pressure, chemistry, and ordinary radiation — only nuclear reactions change them.

rows.definition: A sequence of radioactive decays in which one nucleus changes into another, which may decay again, and so on until a stable nucleus is reached. Every step makes a different nucleus. Nature has several long chains, for example the uranium-238 chain, which ends in stable lead-206, and the thorium-232 chain, which ends in stable lead-208. Radon is one link in the uranium chain.
quick_facts: One unstable nucleus can start a whole chain
Each step makes a different nucleus
The chain ends at a stable nucleus
The uranium-238 chain ends in stable lead-206
The thorium-232 chain ends in stable lead-208

sources.title: Natural decay series (candidate source: open and confirm before publish)

rows.debunking_snippet: “Every decay makes a stable atom.” Many decays only make another unstable nucleus, so the chain goes on.

rows.definition: The central safety philosophy of nuclear engineering: never rely on a single barrier or system, because everything can fail. Safety is layered five ways — prevent abnormal operation, control accidents within systems, contain severe damage, manage core melt, and plan emergency response — wrapped around a chain of physical barriers: the ceramic fuel pellet itself, the metal cladding around it, the steel reactor vessel, and finally the containment building. Any one layer can fail; no plausible scenario fails them all at once.
quick_facts: Multiple independent layers — no single point of failure
Physical barriers: fuel pellet → cladding → reactor vessel → containment
Five operational levels from prevention to emergency response
Redundant + diverse safety systems that back each other up
Codified in IAEA safety principles worldwide
rows.debunking_snippet: “Nuclear plants are safe only if nothing ever goes wrong.” The design assumes things WILL go wrong — equipment failures, operator errors, even floods — and layers backup after backup on top of each failure.

rows.definition: DNA is the genetic material in living cells. Ionizing radiation has enough energy to affect the atoms in living cells, and so it can damage DNA. Cells are extremely efficient at repairing this damage, but if it is not repaired correctly a cell may die or eventually become cancerous.
quick_facts: The genetic material inside living cells
Ionizing radiation can damage it
Cells are extremely efficient at repairing the damage
rows.debunking_snippet: “Radiation damage to a cell can never be undone.” The cells in our bodies are extremely efficient at repairing this damage.

rows.definition: How fast radiation dose accumulates — e.g. microsieverts per hour (μsv/h) or millisieverts per year (mSv/yr). Rate matters biologically: the body can repair low-intensity damage over hours and days, so the same total dose spread over a year is far less harmful than delivered all at once. Natural background averages roughly 0.27 μSv/h worldwide; regulatory limits for nuclear workers (20 mSv/yr averaged) are built entirely around dose-rate thinking.
quick_facts: Dose per unit time: μSv/h, mSv/yr
Natural background ≈ 0.27 μSv/h averaged globally
Same total dose is safer when spread out — the body repairs damage
Drives occupational limits: 20 mSv/yr averaged over 5 years
What survey meters and area monitors actually display
rows.debunking_snippet: “A hot reading means immediate danger.” Not without the time dimension — 10 μSv/h for an hour-long visit is trivial; the same spot for a full year is a different story.

rows.definition: A device worn by radiation workers to record the cumulative ionizing-radiation dose they receive. Passive types — film badges, thermoluminescent (TLD), and optically stimulated luminescent (OSL) dosimeters — are read out periodically, typically monthly. Direct-reading electronic dosimeters show live dose and dose-rate with alarms. Legal limits make them mandatory for classified workers in medicine, nuclear power, research, and industry.
quick_facts: Records cumulative personal radiation dose
Passive types: film badge, TLD, OSL — read monthly or quarterly
Electronic types show real-time dose and dose-rate with alarms
Legally required for classified radiation workers
Worn on the torso; special versions for fingers (ring badges)
rows.debunking_snippet: “A Geiger counter and a dosimeter are the same thing.” They're not — a Geiger counter detects radiation instantly but forgets; a dosimeter remembers your accumulated dose over weeks and months.

rows.definition: Hungarian-American theoretical physicist (1908–2003), known as the 'father of the hydrogen bomb'. After fleeing Nazi Germany and working on the Manhattan Project's fission weapons, he drove the 1951 Ulam–Teller staged-compression idea that made thermonuclear weapons feasible — the Ivy Mike shot (1952) proved it. He co-founded Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory and championed nuclear weapons testing, rocket propulsion, and civil defense. His 1954 testimony that Robert Oppenheimer was a security risk split the scientific community and remains controversial.
quick_facts: 'Father of the hydrogen bomb' — Ulam–Teller design, tested 1952
Worked on the Manhattan Project's fission bombs
Co-founded Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (1952)
Testified against Oppenheimer in 1954, dividing scientists
Lifelong advocate of nuclear deterrence and testing
rows.debunking_snippet: “The hydrogen bomb was one man's invention.” It took many hands — Stanisław Ulam's compression scheme was as essential as Teller's vision; both names are on the key 1951 paper.

rows.definition: The force between electric charges. Opposite charges pull together and like charges push apart. In an atom it pulls the electrons toward the nucleus. Inside the nucleus it pushes the positive protons away from each other, and the strong force has to hold them together.
quick_facts: Like charges push apart and opposite charges pull together
It keeps electrons around the nucleus
It pushes the protons in a nucleus apart
Between particles it is far stronger than gravity
It is also called the Coulomb force

rows.definition: Energy that travels as waves of electric and magnetic fields. It is not made of matter. Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are all electromagnetic radiation. They differ in how much energy they carry. Gamma rays carry far more energy than visible light.
quick_facts: Light is electromagnetic radiation
Gamma rays are electromagnetic radiation too
It is energy, not matter
Different kinds carry different amounts of energy
Alpha and beta are particles, not electromagnetic radiation
rows.debunking_snippet: “Radiation always means nuclear radiation.” Light is radiation too. Only some radiation comes from nuclei.

rows.definition: A fundamental subatomic particle carrying the smallest unit of negative electric charge, discovered by J.J. Thomson in 1897. Electrons aren't little balls circling the nucleus like planets — they exist as probability clouds (orbitals) whose shapes define chemistry. With just 1/1836 of a proton's mass, they're easily knocked loose, which is what electricity, chemical bonds, and beta radiation are all about.
quick_facts: Discovered by J.J. Thomson (1897)
Charge: −1 · mass only 1/1836 of a proton
Occupy orbitals — probability clouds, not orbits
Their arrangement determines an element's chemistry
A free electron emitted from a nucleus is beta radiation
rows.debunking_snippet: “Electrons spin around the nucleus like planets around the Sun.” That's a 100-year-old classroom picture. Quantum mechanics replaced it with orbitals: smeared-out probability clouds where an electron has no definite path.

rows.definition: A picture of where the electrons of an atom are found. Instead of racing around the nucleus on neat rings, the electrons are somewhere in a fuzzy region around it. The cloud is darker where an electron is more likely to be. The cloud is huge compared with the nucleus, so most of an atom is empty space.
quick_facts: It replaces the old picture of electrons as tiny planets
Darker parts show where an electron is more likely to be
The cloud is about 100,000 times wider than the nucleus
Each shape of cloud is called an orbital
rows.debunking_snippet: “Electrons circle the nucleus like planets.” They have no fixed path. The cloud shows where they are likely to be.

rows.definition: A pure substance made of only one kind of atom: every atom of an element has the same number of protons. Hydrogen, carbon, oxygen and gold are elements. About 118 elements are known, and the periodic table lists them in order of atomic number.
quick_facts: Every atom of an element has the same number of protons
About 118 elements are known
The periodic table lists them in order of atomic number
Atoms of one element can differ in neutrons: those are isotopes
Change the number of protons and you change the element
rows.debunking_snippet: “Elements are made of different kinds of stuff.” Every atom is built from the same three particles. Only the number of protons is different.

rows.definition: Concentrating the fissile uranium-235 fraction above its stingy 0.7% natural abundance. Because isotopes share identical chemistry, separation exploits tiny mass differences: thousands of spinning gas centrifuges feed UF₆ through cascades, each stage nudging the ratio upward. Reactor fuel lands at 3–5%, research reactors may want 20%, and weapons-grade means >90%. The same machines serve both ends — which makes every centrifuge plant a proliferation question.
quick_facts: Natural U-235: only 0.72%
Light-water reactor fuel: 3–5% enriched
Weapons-grade: >90% — a long technical leap beyond reactor fuel
Gas centrifuges replaced gaseous diffusion worldwide
Effort measured in Separative Work Units (SWU)
rows.debunking_snippet: “Any country with enrichment can quickly build a bomb.” Reactor-grade (3–5%) to weapons-grade (>90%) is an enormous engineering, energy, and detection challenge — that gap is exactly what IAEA inspectors police.

rows.definition: Italian-American physicist (1901–1954), arguably the last great physicist at home in both theory and experiment. He won the 1938 Nobel Prize for discovering nuclear reactions induced by slow neutrons, then — after fleeing fascist Italy's racial laws — directed the construction of Chicago Pile-1, the world's first self-sustaining chain reaction (December 2, 1942), under Arthur Compton's Met Lab. Fermions, fermium, Fermilab, and the Fermi paradox all carry his name.
quick_facts: Built Chicago Pile-1, the first reactor (Dec 2, 1942)
Nobel Prize in Physics (1938) for slow-neutron work
Left Italy in 1938 over anti-Jewish laws affecting his wife
Element fermium, 'fermions', and Fermilab honor him
Co-designed the pile with Leo Szilard on the team

rows.definition: American physicist (1901–1958) who invented the cyclotron in 1930 — the first accelerator practical enough to smash atoms productively — winning the 1939 Nobel Prize in Physics. His Radiation Laboratory at Berkeley became the birthplace of accelerator-based science; it spun off the discovery of technetium, plutonium, and hundreds of radioisotopes, and later evolved into today's Lawrence Berkeley and Lawrence Livermore national laboratories. Element 103, lawrencium, is named for him.
quick_facts: Invented the cyclotron (1930)
Nobel Prize in Physics (1939)
His lab discovered technetium and helped isolate plutonium
Berkeley and Livermore national labs bear his name
Element 103 — lawrencium — honors him

rows.definition: New Zealand-born British physicist (1871–1937), the father of nuclear physics. He identified alpha and beta radiation (and named gamma), won the 1908 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for radioactivity research, discovered the atomic nucleus with his 1911 gold-foil experiment, and in 1919 achieved the first artificial nuclear reaction — knocking protons out of nitrogen — which earned him credit as the first person to deliberately split the atom. He also named the proton.
quick_facts: Discovered the atomic nucleus (gold foil, 1911)
Nobel Prize in Chemistry (1908) for radioactivity
Named alpha, beta, and gamma radiation
First artificial nuclear reaction: nitrogen + alpha (1919)
Coined the word 'proton'

rows.definition: Irish physicist (1903–1995) who, with John Cockcroft, built the first particle accelerator able to disintegrate atomic nuclei. In 1932 at Cambridge they fired protons at lithium and watched it split into two helium nuclei — the first deliberate splitting of the atom by artificially accelerated particles, and the first direct confirmation of E = mc² on a nuclear scale. The two shared the 1951 Nobel Prize in Physics; their Cockcroft–Walton voltage multiplier still serves as the front end of modern accelerators.
quick_facts: Split lithium with protons — first artificial atom-splitting (1932)
Shared the 1951 Nobel Prize in Physics with Cockcroft
Cockcroft–Walton generator: still used to inject accelerators
First laboratory test of E = mc² in nuclear reactions
Ireland's only physics Nobel laureate

rows.definition: Hungarian-American theoretical physicist (1902–1995) who won the 1963 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on the theory of the atomic nucleus and elementary particles, especially symmetry principles. A Manhattan Project veteran, he led the design team behind the Hanford plutonium-production reactors and co-invented the pressurized water reactor with Alvin Weinberg. He also described the 'Wigner effect' — neutron damage to graphite — and applied group theory so deeply to physics that colleagues called him 'the Silent Genius'.
quick_facts: Nobel Prize in Physics (1963) for nuclear & symmetry theory
Led the design of the Hanford production reactors
Co-patented the pressurized water reactor with Weinberg
Identified the Wigner effect: neutrons damaging graphite
Brought group theory into the heart of quantum physics

rows.definition: Being subjected to radiation — externally (sources outside the body: X-ray machines, cosmic rays) or internally (inhaled or ingested emitters like radon or iodine-131). Strictly speaking, 'exposure' is also a precise legacy unit: the roentgen measured ionization produced in air by X-rays. In everyday safety talk it just means dose received, minimized by the golden trio: time (less of it), distance (more of it), shielding (more of it).
quick_facts: External: sources outside your body
Internal: breathed or eaten emitters — like radon
Strict definition: ionization in air (the old roentgen)
Reduce with time, distance, and shielding
Everyone gets some every day — background is unavoidable
rows.debunking_snippet: “Standing near a source means you're contaminated.” No — external exposure leaves nothing behind. Contamination means actual radioactive material ON or IN you; a sunburn isn't a tan made of sunshine.

rows.definition: French physicist (1900–1958) who ran the laboratory alongside his wife — and fellow Nobel laureate — Irène Joliot-Curie, daughter of Marie and Pierre Curie. In 1934 the couple bombarded aluminum with alpha particles and produced phosphorus-30: the first artificially created radioactive material. It opened the door to making radioisotopes on demand for medicine and research, and earned both of them the 1935 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Frédéric later founded France's Atomic Energy Commission (CEA) and filed some of the earliest nuclear-reactor patent concepts.
quick_facts: Created the first artificial radioactivity (1934)
Shared the 1935 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Irène
Their trick: alpha-bombard aluminum → radioactive phosphorus-30
Founded France's CEA after World War II
Trained in the lab of Marie Curie — whom he married into

rows.definition: Long sealed metal tubes — typically zirconium alloy — packed with ceramic pellets of enriched uranium dioxide, each about the size of a fingertip. The rods are bundled into fuel assemblies that stand inside the reactor core, where fission in the pellets generates heat. The ceramic pellet survives temperatures near 2,800 °C and traps most fission products inside it; the cladding tube around it is the second physical barrier in defense-in-depth, keeping radioactive material sealed away from the coolant.
quick_facts: Ceramic uranium-dioxide pellets inside zircon-alloy tubes
Pellets melt only around 2,800 °C and retain fission products
Rods bundle into assemblies standing in the reactor core
Cladding = second barrier of defense-in-depth
Replaced roughly every 4–6 years as spent fuel
rows.debunking_snippet: “Nuclear fuel rods are glowing green bars.” Real fuel looks like plain gray ceramic pellets stacked in metal tubes — it isn't even noticeably radioactive before it goes into the reactor.

rows.definition: High-energy electromagnetic radiation given off by a nucleus, usually right after an alpha or beta decay leaves it with extra energy. Gamma radiation is not a particle and is not made of pieces of the nucleus. It is like light, but far more energetic. Giving off gamma radiation changes neither the number of protons nor the number of neutrons.
quick_facts: It is electromagnetic radiation, not a particle
It is like light, but far more energetic
It carries away extra energy from the nucleus
The nucleus keeps the same protons and neutrons
It is not made of tiny pieces of the nucleus
rows.debunking_snippet: “Gamma radiation is made of tiny pieces of the nucleus.” It is electromagnetic radiation, like light but far more energetic.

rows.definition: The most penetrating form of radiation: a high-energy photon with no mass and no charge, traveling at the speed of light. Gamma rays pour out of unstable nuclei that still have excess energy after emitting an alpha or beta particle. They pass through the body easily, need centimeters of lead or meters of concrete for shielding, and ionize atoms along the way — which makes them both a hazard and a tool, from sterilizing medical equipment to treating tumors.
quick_facts: High-energy photons: no mass, no charge, speed of light
Emitted when a nucleus sheds leftover energy after decay
Shielded by lead or concrete — never fully 'stopped', only attenuated
Sterilizes ~40% of the world's single-use medical devices
Cobalt-60 gamma beams treat cancer (teletherapy)
rows.debunking_snippet: “Gamma rays make things radioactive.” At normal energies they don't — gamma irradiation adds energy, not radioactivity. That's exactly why food can be irradiated safely: nothing becomes radioactive; microbes are simply killed.

rows.definition: A portable radiation detector built around a gas-filled tube: when ionizing radiation passes through, it triggers a brief electrical avalanche counted as one click or blip. Invented by Hans Geiger in 1908 and refined with Walther Müller in 1928 into the rugged Geiger–Müller tube used everywhere from power plants to prospecting. With the right window it detects alpha, beta, and gamma radiation — though it only counts events, never telling you their energy.
quick_facts: Counts ionization pulses from a gas-filled tube
Geiger–Müller design dates to 1928
Detects alpha (thin window), beta, and gamma
Reports counts — not energy or full dose by itself
Cheap, rugged, and instantly readable
rows.debunking_snippet: “If the clicking stops, it's safe.” Dangerous trap: in extreme fields a Geiger tube saturates and goes quiet while radiation is at its worst. Silence is not safety.

rows.definition: American chemist (1912–1999) who discovered plutonium in 1941 and went on to share in the identification of ten transuranium elements, work honored with the 1951 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (with Edwin McMillan). He proposed the actinide concept that reshaped the periodic table's bottom row, advised ten presidents — including chairing the AEC under Kennedy and Johnson — and remains the only person to have a chemical element (seaborgium) named after him while still alive.
quick_facts: Co-discovered plutonium (1941)
Nobel Prize in Chemistry (1951, with McMillan)
Credited with 10 transuranium elements
His actinide concept reshaped the periodic table
Only person with an element named after them in their lifetime

rows.definition: Elements heavier than uranium (Z > 93): neptunium through oganesson. All are radioactive, and none survive meaningfully from Earth's formation — they exist because stars, cosmic rays, reactors, and bombs keep making them. Seaborg's team synthesized plutonium and nine others between 1940 and 1974, and trace amounts arise naturally in ore bodies too (even the ancient Oklo reactor cooked up some plutonium). Their short lifetimes and rising instability with size mark chemistry's practical frontier.
quick_facts: All elements beyond Z = 92: neptunium → oganesson (118)
Every one is radioactive
Made by neutron bombardment followed by beta decay
Named for scientists, places, and planets
Trace amounts occur naturally — even Oklo's fossil reactor made some

rows.definition: The SI unit of absorbed radiation dose: 1 Gy means one joule of radiation energy deposited per kilogram of material, adopted in 1975 and named after British physicist Louis Harold Gray, a pioneer of radiation dosimetry. It replaced the older rad (1 Gy = 100 rad). Gray measures pure physical energy absorption — to gauge biological harm, sieverts weight each radiation type by its effectiveness.
quick_facts: 1 Gy = 1 joule per kilogram
Adopted as an SI unit in 1975; replaces the rad (1 Gy = 100 rad)
Named after dosimetry pioneer Louis Harold Gray
Physical unit — biological risk needs sieverts
Medical doses quoted in Gy: e.g., ~2 Gy per radiotherapy fraction

rows.definition: The time it takes for half of the atoms in a radioactive sample to decay — and then half of what's left in the next interval, and so on. Decay is a pure exponential: after two half-lives a quarter survives, after three an eighth. Every isotope has its own fixed value, from fractions of a second (polonium-212) to billions of years (uranium-238). It cannot practically be altered by temperature, pressure, or chemistry — which makes half-life a dependable clock for dating everything from ancient wood to Earth's oldest rocks.
quick_facts: Time for half of a sample's atoms to decay
Exponential: 2 half-lives → ¼ left, 3 → ⅛
Ranges from milliseconds (Po-212) to billions of years (U-238)
Iodine-131: 8 days · Carbon-14: 5,700 years · U-238: 4.5 billion
Unchanged by heat, cold, pressure, or chemistry
rows.debunking_snippet: “After two half-lives it's all gone.” After two half-lives a quarter remains, and it keeps halving forever — never quite zero. That's why waste storage is measured in many half-lives.

rows.definition: German-American physicist (1906–2005) who worked out how stars shine: in 1939 he described the proton–proton chain and CNO cycle that fuse hydrogen into helium in stellar cores, earning the 1967 Nobel Prize in Physics. During the Manhattan Project he headed the Theoretical Division at Los Alamos, and later became a measured voice for arms control — opposing the race for more exotic weapons while contributing to their underlying physics.
quick_facts: Explained how stars fuse hydrogen and shine (1939)
Nobel Prize in Physics (1967)
Headed the Theory Division at Los Alamos
Developed both the p-p chain and CNO cycle models
Later a prominent advocate of arms-control treaties

rows.definition: Water whose hydrogen atoms are swapped for deuterium — hydrogen carrying an extra neutron (D₂O). Chemically almost identical to ordinary water but about 10% denser, it is prized as a reactor moderator because it barely absorbs neutrons at all. That neutron economy lets CANDU reactors run on natural, non-enriched uranium — trading expensive enrichment for expensive D₂O production.
quick_facts: D₂O: hydrogen replaced by deuterium (one extra neutron each)
~10% denser than ordinary water
Absorbs far fewer neutrons than light water
Lets CANDU reactors use natural, un-enriched uranium
Costly: thousands of liters per reactor tonne of moderator
rows.debunking_snippet: “Heavy water is radioactive.” It isn't — deuterium is stable. A sip is harmless (you drink trace amounts daily); it would only matter if it were most of your water for weeks.

rows.definition: French physicist (1852–1908) who discovered radioactivity by accident in 1896: investigating whether uranium salts glow after sunlight exposure, he found they fogged a photographic plate even in a drawer on a cloudy week — the uranium emitted penetrating rays all by itself. Marie and Pierre Curie chased down the phenomenon and coined 'radioactivity'; all three shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics, and the SI activity unit bears his name.
quick_facts: Discovered radioactivity in 1896 — via a cloudy-week accident
Uranium salts fogged plates with no sunlight needed
Shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with the Curies
The becquerel (Bq) unit honors him
Came from a family dynasty of physicists — son and grandson too

rows.definition: A heavily shielded room for hands-off handling of intensely radioactive materials. Workers stay outside lead, steel, or thick concrete walls and manipulate equipment through master-slave mechanical arms while watching through lead-glass windows — dense panes up to a meter thick that still let light through. Hot cells are where spent fuel is examined, medical isotopes are processed, and vitrified waste is packed; nothing inside needs a human body anywhere near it.
quick_facts: Shielded rooms for highly radioactive work
Master-slave manipulator arms reach through walls
Lead-glass viewing windows up to ~1 m thick
Used for spent-fuel research, isotope processing, reprocessing R&D
Air pressure kept negative so nothing leaks outward

rows.definition: U.S. Navy admiral (1900–1986), the 'Father of the Nuclear Navy'. He drove the development of compact pressurized-water propulsion — building on the PWR concept from Weinberg and Wigner — culminating in USS Nautilus (1954), the first nuclear submarine, which sailed under the North Pole in 1958. His obsessive engineering culture, personal interviews of every officer candidate, and insistence on rigorous training shaped naval nuclear safety into one of the safest industries anywhere. He served 63 years — the longest of any U.S. naval officer — and his team later launched the first full-size civilian PWR power plant at Shippingport.
quick_facts: 'Father of the Nuclear Navy'
USS Nautilus: first nuclear submarine (1954), reached North Pole 1958
63 years of service — longest in U.S. Navy history
His safety program has run reactors without major release since the 1950s
Shippingport (1957): first U.S. full-scale civilian nuclear plant

rows.definition: Soviet physicist (1903–1960) who directed the Soviet atomic bomb project — the effort that detonated the USSR's first device, RDS-1, in 1949 and ended America's nuclear monopoly. His institute also delivered Obninsk (1954), the world's first nuclear power plant connected to an electricity grid, years before Britain's Calder Hall. Late in life he publicly urged an end to atmospheric weapons testing, and the Kurchatov Institute — Russia's leading nuclear research center — carries his name.
quick_facts: Directed the Soviet atomic project (RDS-1 tested 1949)
Delivered Obninsk (1954): first grid-connected nuclear power plant
'Father of Soviet atomic energy'
Late-career advocate against atmospheric testing
The Kurchatov Institute is named after him

rows.definition: An atom, or a group of atoms, that has gained or lost electrons, so it carries an electric charge. Losing an electron makes a positive ion and gaining one makes a negative ion. The element does not change, because the number of protons stays the same. Table salt is made of sodium ions and chloride ions.
quick_facts: An ion has a charge because its protons and electrons no longer match
Losing electrons makes a positive ion
Gaining electrons makes a negative ion
The element stays the same: only electrons moved
Ionizing radiation can knock electrons off atoms and make ions
rows.debunking_snippet: “Gaining or losing electrons changes the element.” Protons decide the element, so an ion is still the same element.

rows.definition: A gas-filled radiation detector operating below the Geiger avalanche regime: radiation ionizes the gas and the resulting tiny current — collected between two electrodes — flows in proportion to dose rate. That proportionality makes ion chambers the reference instruments for accurate dosimetry, from calibrating hospital radiotherapy beams to monitoring reactor buildings. The humble household smoke detector runs on the same principle: smoke disrupts a tiny ion chamber's current and triggers the alarm.
quick_facts: Current proportional to dose rate — unlike counting GM tubes
The accuracy standard for radiotherapy beam calibration
No avalanche: linear response across huge ranges
Same principle as household smoke detectors
Can measure energy deposited, not just count events
rows.debunking_snippet: “Geiger counters are the most accurate radiation meters.” They're the loudest, not the most precise — ion chambers are what hospitals and regulators use when the number has to be right.

rows.definition: Radiation carrying enough energy — roughly above 10 electron-volts — to strip electrons from atoms or molecules, leaving charged ions behind. It covers particle radiations (alpha, beta, neutrons) and high-frequency electromagnetic waves (X-rays, gamma rays); visible light and radio fall below the line. In living tissue it damages DNA both directly and indirectly through reactive fragments of water molecules, which is why exposure limits, shielding, and monitoring exist everywhere it's used.
quick_facts: Threshold ~10 eV per interaction
Particle forms: alpha, beta, neutrons · EM forms: X-ray, gamma
Damages DNA directly and via water-derived free radicals
Non-ionizing means safe-ish: UV, light, radio can't break bonds
Basis of medical imaging, sterilization, and cancer therapy
rows.debunking_snippet: “All radiation is dangerous.” Only ionizing radiation breaks chemical bonds. Your Wi-Fi, microwave, and heat lamp are non-ionizing — they lack the energy to rip electrons off atoms.

rows.definition: French chemist and physicist (1897–1956), daughter of Marie and Pierre Curie and, with her husband Frédéric, discoverer of artificial radioactivity in 1934 — earning the 1935 Nobel Prize in Chemistry as only the second woman ever to win one. She served as Undersecretary of State for Scientific Research in post-war France and helped shape early French reactors. Like her mother, she died of a radiation-linked blood disease (leukemia), a consequence of working before protection standards existed.
quick_facts: Co-discovered artificial radioactivity (1934)
Nobel Prize in Chemistry (1935) — second woman so honored
Daughter of Marie and Pierre Curie
France's Undersecretary for Scientific Research (1936)
Died of leukemia linked to early unshielded lab work
rows.debunking_snippet: “Radiation safety rules are bureaucratic overkill.” They were written in the blood of pioneers like Irène Joliot-Curie and her mother — brilliant scientists who handled sources bare-handed because nobody knew better yet.

rows.definition: Exposure to radiation that comes from a source outside the body, such as the X-rays of a medical exposure. External irradiation stops when the radiation source is shielded or when the person moves outside the radiation field. It is different from contamination, which means radioactive material is on or in the person.
quick_facts: Being in the path of radiation from a source
A medical X-ray is irradiation from a source outside the body
External irradiation stops when the source is shielded or you move away
It is not the same as contamination
rows.debunking_snippet: “Being near radiation means you are contaminated.” Irradiation is being in the path of radiation. Contamination is radioactive material on or in you. They are not the same thing.

rows.definition: One of the variants of a chemical element: same number of protons, different numbers of neutrons, so the same chemistry but a different mass. Chemist Frederick Soddy coined the name in 1913 — Greek for 'same place', since isotopes occupy the same spot on the periodic table. Every element has them; some are stable forever (carbon-12), others radioactive and decaying at fixed rates (carbon-14). Which isotope you have determines everything about its nuclear behavior while changing nothing about its chemistry.
quick_facts: Same protons, different neutrons — same element, different mass
Name coined by Frederick Soddy (1913): 'same place' in Greek
Stable examples: carbon-12 · radioactive: carbon-14
Uranium-235 fissions easily; uranium-238 barely does
Radioisotopes power medicine, dating, and tracing
rows.debunking_snippet: “'Isotope' just means radioactive.” No — every element has several isotopes, and the majority are perfectly stable. Radioactive ones are called radionuclides.

rows.definition: American theoretical physicist (1904–1967), scientific director of the Los Alamos Laboratory where the Manhattan Project built the first atomic bombs — hence 'father of the atomic bomb'. After watching Trinity (1945) he recalled the Bhagavad Gita: 'Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds.' He later headed the Atomic Energy Commission's advisory committee and argued against a crash program for the hydrogen bomb — a stance, plus old associations, that cost him his security clearance in a sensational 1954 hearing. The government formally rehabilitated him with the Enrico Fermi Award in 1963.
quick_facts: Directed Los Alamos during the Manhattan Project
'Father of the atomic bomb' — Trinity test, July 16, 1945
Opposed the crash program for the hydrogen bomb
Security clearance revoked after the 1954 hearing
Received the Fermi Award in 1963 as rehabilitation
rows.debunking_snippet: “Oppenheimer invented the atomic bomb.” He didn't build or design it alone — he led and coordinated thousands of scientists. His genius was leadership and judgment as much as physics.

rows.definition: British physicist (1891–1974), student of Ernest Rutherford, who discovered the neutron in 1932 by showing that beryllium bombarded with alpha particles ejected an uncharged particle about as heavy as a proton. Because it carries no charge, the neutron slips straight into nuclei without fighting electrical repulsion — the missing key that made induced fission and chain reactions thinkable within months. The discovery earned him the 1935 Nobel Prize in Physics, and during World War II he headed the British Mission to the Manhattan Project.
quick_facts: Discovered the neutron (1932)
Nobel Prize in Physics (1935)
The neutron's zero charge is what makes fission chains possible
Studied under, then worked alongside, Ernest Rutherford
Headed the British Mission to the Manhattan Project

rows.definition: British physicist (1897–1967) who, with Ernest Walton, built the voltage-multiplier accelerator that achieved the first deliberate splitting of atoms in 1932 — lithium struck by protons broke into two helium nuclei. The work shared the 1951 Nobel Prize in Physics. He went on to found and direct Britain's Harwell nuclear research establishment, contributed to the British atomic bomb, and famously insisted — against critics who called it 'Cockcroft's folly' — on installing filters in the Windscale pile chimneys. When the 1957 fire broke out, those filters caught much of the fallout and likely saved many lives.
quick_facts: First artificial nuclear splitting with Walton (1932)
Nobel Prize in Physics (1951)
Founding director of the Harwell research establishment
Cockcroft–Walton multipliers still inject modern accelerators
His 'folly' chimney filters saved lives in the 1957 Windscale fire

rows.definition: German-born theoretical physicist (1911–1988), a Communist who fled the Nazis for Britain — then became the most valuable Soviet spy inside the American bomb project. At Los Alamos he worked on the implosion calculations for Fat Man; at a now-famous 1947 meeting in London he handed Moscow not only full fission-bomb designs but sketches of early hydrogen-bomb thinking. Arrested in 1950 through decrypted Soviet cables (the VENONA effort) and confessed, he served 14 years in prison, then moved to East Germany to direct a physics institute.
quick_facts: Manhattan Project physicist — worked on the implosion bomb
Passed fission-bomb designs and early H-bomb ideas to the USSR
Caught via decrypted Soviet cables (VENONA)
Arrested 1950; served 14 years
His espionage accelerated the first Soviet bomb by years

rows.definition: Hungarian-American physicist (1898–1964) who dreamed up the nuclear chain reaction while crossing a London street in September 1933 — the day after Rutherford dismissed atomic energy as 'moonshine'. He kept the idea secret under a patent, co-invented the reactor concept with Enrico Fermi, and in August 1939 drafted the Einstein–Szilard letter that warned President Roosevelt of possible German bombs and launched what became the Manhattan Project. Horrified by the results, he organized the 1945 scientists' petition against bombing Japanese cities and spent his later years on arms control and molecular biology.
quick_facts: Conceived the chain reaction at a London crosswalk (1933)
Co-patented the nuclear reactor with Fermi
Drafted the Einstein–Szilard letter to Roosevelt (1939)
Circulated a 1945 petition against bombing Japanese cities
Switched careers to biology after the war
rows.debunking_snippet: “The Einstein letter was Einstein's idea.” It was Szilard's from start to finish — Einstein only signed, having barely heard of chain reactions before that morning.

rows.definition: A particle accelerator that pushes charged particles down a straight tube using oscillating electromagnetic fields, adding a kick each segment. Medical LINACs accelerate electrons to millions of electron-volts and slam them into metal targets to produce precisely shaped X-ray beams for cancer radiotherapy — the machine behind most modern radiation oncology. In research, giant LINACs serve as injectors for synchrotrons and as precision probes of nuclear structure.
quick_facts: Accelerates particles in a straight line
The workhorse machine of modern cancer radiotherapy
Medical units: electrons at 6–25 MeV → therapeutic X-rays
Also serves as the injector front-end for big research machines
Microwave cavities give particles repeated energy kicks
rows.debunking_snippet: “Radiotherapy machines are experimental.” Modern LINACs deliver sub-millimeter-guided beams daily in thousands of hospitals — they're among the most precise routinely-used devices in medicine.

rows.definition: Austrian-Swedish physicist (1878–1968) who explained nuclear fission. After fleeing Nazi Germany in July 1938, she received a letter from her longtime collaborator Otto Hahn describing baffling results: neutron-bombarded uranium seemed to produce barium. Walking a winter forest with her nephew Otto Frisch over Christmas, she worked out the physics — the nucleus had split — and Frisch named it 'fission' after biology. The 1944 Chemistry Nobel went to Hahn alone; Meitner's exclusion is science's most cited injustice. She refused to work on weapons: 'I will have nothing to do with a bomb!'
quick_facts: Gave fission its theoretical explanation (Dec 1938)
Coined the term 'fission' with her nephew Otto Frisch
Fled Nazi Germany in July 1938 after 30 years in Berlin
Excluded from the 1944 Nobel Prize given to Hahn alone
Element 109, meitnerium, honors her
rows.debunking_snippet: “She was called the mother of the bomb because she built it.” She did the opposite — when invited to Los Alamos she answered: 'I will have nothing to do with a bomb.' Her contribution was understanding, not weaponry.

rows.definition: The everyday side of radioactive waste: gloves, gowns, filters, tools, labware, and smoke-detector sources — lightly contaminated items from hospitals, research labs, industry, and power plants. It makes up roughly 90% of radioactive waste by volume but only about 1% of its total radioactivity. Most of it decays to background within hours to years and goes into engineered near-surface disposal cells with monitored caps and drains.
quick_facts: ~90% of radioactive waste volume, ~1% of its radioactivity
Includes hospital, laboratory, and industrial items
Often decays to background within hours or years
Disposed in engineered near-surface facilities
Segregated and tracked from cradle to grave
rows.debunking_snippet: “All nuclear waste is glowing drums destined for deep mountains.” The overwhelming majority by volume is low-level waste — contaminated paper, plastic, and filters — safely buried a few meters underground.

rows.definition: Polish-French physicist and chemist (1867–1934), pioneer of radioactivity — a word she herself coined. She discovered polonium and radium in 1898, shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel, and won the 1911 Nobel Prize in Chemistry alone — making her the first woman Nobel laureate, the only person to win Nobels in two different sciences, and mother of another laureate, Irène. She worked with vials of radium on her desk and died of aplastic anemia almost certainly caused by her exposure.
quick_facts: Coined the term 'radioactivity'
Discovered polonium and radium (1898)
Nobel Prizes in two sciences: Physics (1903), Chemistry (1911)
Her notebooks are still radioactive — kept in lead-lined boxes
Died of aplastic anemia from decades of unprotected work
rows.debunking_snippet: “Curie's own notes are dangerous.” True, literally: her century-old notebooks carry radium contamination and can only be viewed with signed waivers — a stark reminder that radiation safety was learned at great cost.

rows.definition: The measured shortfall between a nucleus's actual mass and the added-up masses of its free protons and neutrons. That missing mass didn't vanish — it became binding energy via E = mc² when the nucleus formed. A helium-4 nucleus is about 0.7% lighter than its parts, worth roughly 28 MeV. The bigger the defect per nucleon, the tighter the nucleus is bound and the more stable it is — which is exactly why fission and fusion release energy as they climb toward iron.
quick_facts: Nucleus weighs less than its separated parts
Missing mass converted to binding energy via E = mc²
Helium-4: ~0.7% mass loss = ~28 MeV
Measured with mass spectrometers of extraordinary precision
Predicts stability — and which reactions release energy
rows.debunking_snippet: “Mass is always conserved.” Not quite — mass-energy is. Every nuclear reaction that powers stars, reactors, and bombs trades a sliver of mass for enormous energy.

rows.definition: The total number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus. It is the number written after an element's name: carbon-14 has a mass number of 14. To find the neutrons, take away the protons. Carbon has 6 protons, so carbon-14 has 8 neutrons. The mass number is not the same as the atomic number, which counts only protons.
quick_facts: Mass number = protons + neutrons
It is written after the name, as in uranium-235
Neutrons = mass number minus atomic number
Isotopes of one element have different mass numbers
Electrons weigh so little that they are not counted
rows.debunking_snippet: “The number in carbon-14 is the number of neutrons.” It counts protons and neutrons together. Carbon always has 6 protons, so carbon-14 has 8 neutrons.

rows.definition: Anything that has mass and takes up space. Solids, liquids and gases are all matter, and so is air. All matter is made of atoms. Light and heat are not matter: they are forms of energy. Sound is not matter either, but a wave that travels through matter.
quick_facts: Matter has mass and takes up space
Solids, liquids and gases are all matter
Air is matter: a pumped-up ball weighs more than a flat one
Light and heat are energy, not matter
All matter is made of atoms

sources.title: Chemistry 2e: Phases and Classification of Matter

rows.debunking_snippet: “Air is nothing.” Air is matter. It is made of atoms joined in tiny groups, it has mass, and it takes up space.

rows.definition: A severe accident in which reactor fuel overheats after cooling is lost and begins to melt. The sequence runs fast: if water flow stops, temperatures climb within seconds-to-minutes, zirconium cladding reacts with steam above ~1,200 °C producing hydrogen, and the ceramic fuel itself doesn't liquefy until near 2,800 °C. It has happened three times commercially — Three Mile Island (1979, half the core, zero deaths, fully contained), Chernobyl (1986, no full containment), Fukushima (2011, hydrogen explosions).
quick_facts: Loss of cooling — not loss of control — drives most meltdown risk
Cladding fails ~1,200 °C; fuel melts near 2,800 °C
Zirconium + steam makes the hydrogen behind Fukushima's blasts
TMI's partial meltdown killed no one; containment held
Modern designs add passive cooling that works unpowered
rows.debunking_snippet: “A meltdown means thousands die instantly.” The worst-case isn't automatic: TMI's core half-melted and harmed no one — because containment did its job. Consequences depend entirely on barriers, not just the melting itself.

rows.definition: A millisievert (mSv) is one thousandth of a sievert, the unit used to count a radiation dose. Everyday doses are small, so they are usually given in millisieverts. The average person in the United States gets about 6.2 millisieverts a year, and most of it is natural background radiation.
quick_facts: One thousandth of a sievert
1 sievert is 1000 millisieverts
The average yearly dose in the United States is about 6.2 millisieverts
rows.debunking_snippet: “A radiation number is always frightening.” A number only means something with its unit and a comparison. About 6.2 millisieverts is an average year in the United States, and about 1000 in a short time is where illness starts.

rows.definition: A material that slows the fast neutrons born from fission (speeds around 20,000 km/s) down to 'thermal' speeds of a couple of kilometers per second — the pace at which uranium-235 captures them billions of times more readily. Good moderators bounce neutrons without absorbing many: ordinary water (the most common), heavy water, and graphite. Water does double duty in most reactors, cooling the fuel while moderating the chain reaction.
quick_facts: Slows neutrons from ~20,000 km/s to ~2 km/s
Thermal neutrons split U-235 far more efficiently
Light water, heavy water, and graphite are the classics
Lose the moderator and most reactors simply stop — a safety feature
Chernobyl's RBMK was the rare design that could run un-moderated
rows.debunking_snippet: “Reactors need everything to go right to stay running.” For most designs the opposite holds: lose the water moderator and the physics itself shuts the chain down — no operator required.

rows.definition: American theoretical physicist (1929–2019) who brought order to the particle zoo. His 1961 'eightfold way' sorted hadrons into families by symmetry, then in 1964 he proposed that protons and neutrons are built from three fractionally-charged constituents he named quarks — a word he lifted from Joyce's Finnegans Wake ('Three quarks for Muster Mark!'). The quark model earned him the 1969 Nobel Prize in Physics and remains the backbone of our picture of matter's deepest layer.
quick_facts: Proposed the quark model (1964)
Named 'quark' from James Joyce's Finnegans Wake
Nobel Prize in Physics (1969)
Earlier devised the 'eightfold way' classification of particles
Also co-founded complexity science at Santa Fe Institute

rows.definition: The neutral particle sharing the atomic nucleus with protons — almost exactly as heavy (1.67×10⁻²⁷ kg), just 0.14% heavier, and carrying no electric charge. That neutrality is its superpower: it slips through electron clouds and into nuclei without electrical resistance, which makes it both the trigger of fission chains and a deep-penetrating probe of matter. Freed from a nucleus a neutron survives about 15 minutes before decaying into a proton, an electron, and an antineutrino.
quick_facts: Zero charge · mass 0.14% above the proton's
James Chadwick discovered it (1932)
Free neutrons decay in ~15 minutes
Only slow ('thermal') neutrons efficiently split U-235
Neutrons damage crystal lattices — the 'Wigner effect'
rows.debunking_snippet: “Neutrons are dangerous because they're charged.” The opposite — their danger comes from having no charge at all: nothing repels them, so they penetrate deeply and can even turn stable atoms radioactive.

rows.definition: Danish physicist (1885–1962) who in 1913 gave the atom its first workable quantum picture — electrons in fixed orbits jumping between energy levels — earning the 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics. His Copenhagen institute became the crossroads of quantum physics, and his liquid-droplet model of the nucleus was exactly what Lise Meitner used to explain fission in 1938. After fleeing occupied Denmark in 1943 he consulted on the Manhattan Project and later championed openness between nations about nuclear matters.
quick_facts: Bohr model of the atom (1913)
Nobel Prize in Physics (1922)
Founded his Copenhagen institute in 1921
His droplet model explained how fission happens
Escaped Denmark by fishing boat in 1943
rows.debunking_snippet: “Bohr's planetary atom is still the accepted model.” It was a stepping stone — replaced within a decade by full quantum mechanics and orbitals, though it remains the perfect first sketch.

rows.definition: The splitting of a heavy nucleus — uranium-235, plutonium-239 — into two unequal fragments plus 2–3 spare neutrons and about 200 million electron-volts of energy. Hahn and Strassmann spotted the barium evidence in late 1938; Meitner and Frisch explained it months later. Each released neutron can split another nucleus, enabling chain reactions that either simmer steadily in a reactor or multiply explosively in a weapon. The fragments themselves are intensely radioactive — which is where spent-fuel heat and waste come from.
quick_facts: ~200 MeV released per U-235 fission
Typical split: one heavy fragment (~140 amu) + one lighter (~95 amu)
Discovered 1938; explained early 1939
Both fragments are radioactive — hence reactor waste
Runs reactors today and could burn waste tomorrow

rows.definition: Joining two light nuclei — usually hydrogen isotopes — into a heavier one, converting the mass difference to energy. Per kilogram of fuel, fusion releases roughly four times more energy than fission (though each single reaction carries less punch than one fission). It powers every star, including our Sun, whose core squeezes protons together at 15 million °C against their mutual repulsion. On Earth, magnetic bottles (tokamaks like ITER) and laser implosions chase net energy, with deuterium–tritium the easiest first target.
quick_facts: ~4× more energy per kg of fuel than fission
Powers all stars — the Sun fuses 600 million tonnes of H every second
Needs stellar temperatures: millions of degrees minimum
D–T fusion: 17.6 MeV per reaction, mostly as a fast neutron
Main 'waste' is short-lived activated metal, not millennia-old fuel
rows.debunking_snippet: “Each fusion reaction out-energizes each fission.” Individually it doesn't — 17.6 MeV versus ~200 MeV per event. Fusion's advantage is per kilogram of fuel, thanks to light nuclei packing more binding-energy gain.

rows.definition: A machine holding a nuclear chain reaction at exactly critical — steady — power. Fuel assemblies of enriched uranium sit in a lattice with moderator and coolant while control rods trim reactivity; heat from fission boils water or gas to spin turbines. Around 440 power reactors supply roughly a tenth of world electricity with near-zero carbon, and specialized designs produce medical isotopes, research beams, and naval propulsion. Physics itself leans safe: most designs shut down if cooling or moderation is lost.
quick_facts: ≈440 power reactors worldwide — ~10% of global electricity
Fuel: 3–5% enriched uranium — far below weapons grade
Control rods, moderator, and coolant keep k exactly 1
Also built for ships, research, and medical isotopes
Life-cycle carbon comparable to wind power
rows.debunking_snippet: “A reactor can detonate like an atomic bomb.” Physically impossible — bomb fuel is >90% enriched and assembled supercritically in microseconds; reactor fuel is dilute ceramic that can't sustain that.

rows.definition: Whether a nucleus stays as it is or will change one day. A nucleus is stable when the strong force that holds it together balances the electric push between its protons. Stability depends on the mix of protons and neutrons: each element has only a few neutron counts that give a stable nucleus. Most atoms around us are stable. The others are unstable, which means radioactive.
quick_facts: Stable: the nucleus stays as it is
Unstable: the nucleus will change and give off radiation
It depends on the mix of protons and neutrons
Carbon-12 and carbon-13 are stable, but carbon-14 is not
Most atoms around us are stable

sources.title: University Physics Volume 3: Nuclear Binding Energy

rows.debunking_snippet: “More neutrons always make a nucleus safer.” Too many neutrons can unbalance a nucleus too, as in carbon-14.

rows.definition: The positively charged core of an atom, made of protons and neutrons bound together by the strong nuclear force. It holds more than 99.9% of the atom's mass while spanning only about 1/100,000 of the atom's diameter — matter at this density would weigh hundreds of millions of tonnes per cubic centimeter. Ernest Rutherford discovered the nucleus in 1911 by firing alpha particles at gold foil and finding that a rare few bounced straight back.
quick_facts: Discovered by Ernest Rutherford (1911, gold-foil experiment)
Diameter ~100,000 times smaller than the atom itself
Holds over 99.9% of the atom's mass
Protons and neutrons bound by the strong nuclear force
Home of radioactive decay and all nuclear reactions

rows.definition: Austrian-British physicist (1904–1979), Lise Meitner's nephew and her partner in the Christmas 1938 forest walk where they worked out that Hahn's barium meant the nucleus had split — Frisch borrowed 'fission' from biology for the name. Weeks later he confirmed it experimentally with recoil bursts from neutron-blasted uranium. In 1940 his memorandum with Rudolf Peierls estimated a critical mass of pure U-235 at roughly kilograms, not tons — the calculation that first made atomic bombs seem buildable. He joined the British Mission at Los Alamos afterward.
quick_facts: Explained fission with Lise Meitner (Dec 1938)
Borrowed the word 'fission' from cell biology
Experimentally confirmed fission within weeks
Frisch–Peierls memo (1940): first serious bomb feasibility study
Worked at Los Alamos as part of the British Mission

rows.definition: German radiochemist (1879–1968) whose careful chemistry proved nuclear fission: in December 1938 he and Fritz Strassmann found barium — half an atom's worth of weight — inside neutron-bombarded uranium, a result so strange Hahn hesitated to publish. The discovery earned him the 1944 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (awarded in 1945). With Lise Meitner he had spent three decades discovering isotopes including protactinium, but she was barred by Nazi law from co-authorship and later from sharing credit — a controversy that shadows his legacy.
quick_facts: Proved nuclear fission with Strassmann (Dec 1938)
Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1944 (presented 1945)
Discovered protactinium and dozens of radioisotopes with Meitner
'Father of nuclear chemistry'
His exclusion of Meitner remains a famous scientific injustice
rows.debunking_snippet: “Hahn invented the atomic bomb.” He identified barium atoms in a beaker — brilliant, purely scientific work done before the war, and he refused to work on German weapons research.

rows.definition: The nucleus that decays in a radioactive decay. It is unstable. When it changes, it turns into a different nucleus, called the daughter, and gives off radiation. Nobody has to start the change: the parent changes by itself, at a moment nobody can predict for one nucleus.
quick_facts: The parent is the nucleus that decays
It is unstable
It changes into the daughter and gives off radiation
It changes by itself
In a decay chain, each daughter becomes the next parent
rows.debunking_snippet: “A radioactive atom needs a person to make it decay.” The parent changes by itself. Nobody has to trigger it.

rows.definition: A chart of all the known elements, in order of atomic number. Each box shows an element's atomic number, its symbol and its name. To use it, start with the number of protons and find that box: it names the element. Elements in the same column behave in similar ways, which is where the name comes from.
quick_facts: Elements are listed in order of atomic number
The big number in a box is the atomic number: the number of protons
The letters are a short symbol, such as C for carbon
Elements in the same column behave alike
Dmitri Mendeleev published an early version in 1869

rows.definition: French physicist (1859–1906) who shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with Marie Curie and Henri Becquerel for radioactivity research. As a young man he and his brother Jacques discovered piezoelectricity — the crystal effect now found in quartz watches and ultrasound probes — and built the electrometer Marie used to measure ray intensity. His studies of magnetism gave science the 'Curie temperature', above which materials lose their magnetism. He died in 1906 when a horse-drawn wagon crushed his skull on a Paris street.
quick_facts: Nobel Prize in Physics (1903), shared with Marie and Becquerel
Co-discovered piezoelectricity with his brother Jacques
The Curie temperature marks loss of permanent magnetism
Built the precision instruments behind Marie's measurements
Died in a street accident in Paris (1906), not from radiation
rows.debunking_snippet: “Pierre Curie died of radiation exposure.” No — he was killed instantly by a horse-drawn cart on the rue Dauphine. Radiation took Marie decades later; Pierre simply ran out of luck on a rainy afternoon.

rows.definition: A man-made fissile metal: reactors breed it when uranium-238 captures a neutron and decays twice through neptunium. With a 24,100-year half-life and a bare critical mass near 10 kg, it powers both warheads and recycled reactor fuel (MOX). Chemically unlike anything natural — warm to the touch from its own decay heat — it was discovered by Glenn Seaborg's team in 1941 and sits at the center of both energy policy and non-proliferation politics.
quick_facts: Bred from uranium-238 inside every uranium-fueled reactor
Half-life: 24,100 years
Bare critical mass: only about 10 kg
Recycled with uranium into MOX fuel rods
Discovered by Seaborg's team in 1941
rows.debunking_snippet: “Plutonium is the most toxic substance known.” Folklore. It's radiologically hazardous if inhaled and chemically like other heavy metals — but botulinum toxin and ricin are vastly more poisonous gram-for-gram.

rows.definition: A natural radioactive form of potassium. Only a tiny share of the potassium in nature is potassium-40, but because food and living things contain potassium, a little potassium-40 is in many foods, such as bananas, and in the human body. It has a very long half-life, over a billion years, which is one reason it is still around.
quick_facts: It is a natural radioactive isotope of potassium
A tiny share of all potassium is potassium-40
It is in bananas and other foods
Your own body contains a little
Its half-life is over a billion years

sources.title: Radionuclide Basics: Potassium-40 (candidate source: open and confirm before publish)

rows.debunking_snippet: “Radioactive means dangerous, so bananas are a hazard.” Bananas hold a tiny natural amount, and that is normal. Radioactive does not automatically mean dangerous.

rows.definition: The positively charged particle anchoring every atomic nucleus — +1 charge balancing each electron's −1, and about 1,836 times heavier than an electron. An atom's proton count is its identity card: one makes hydrogen, six carbon, ninety-two uranium. Protons aren't fundamental: each packs three quarks (two 'up', one 'down') bound by gluons, with most of the proton's mass arising from that binding energy. Ernest Rutherford named the proton in 1920 after proving it exists inside nuclei.
quick_facts: +1 charge · ~1,836× electron mass
Count defines the element (Z)
Made of two up quarks + one down quark
Named by Ernest Rutherford (1920)
Experiments bound its lifetime beyond 10³⁴ years
rows.debunking_snippet: “Protons are tiny hard balls.” They're seething bags of quarks and gluons — most of a proton's mass comes from the energy of that internal motion, not the quarks themselves.
