rows.definition: Energy traveling outward from its source — either as electromagnetic waves (radio, infrared, light, UV, X-rays, gamma) or fast particles (alpha, beta, neutrons). The dividing line that matters biologically is energy per quantum: ionizing radiation can tear electrons off atoms and break DNA; non-ionizing radiation mostly just heats things. Radiation is everywhere and always has been — sunlight, rocks, bananas, outer space.
quick_facts: Two families: waves (EM) and particles
Ionizing vs non-ionizing is what matters for health
Bananas are mildly radioactive from potassium-40
Sunlight is radiation — so is Wi-Fi, at very different energies
Background radiation predates humanity by eons
rows.debunking_snippet: “Any amount of radiation is unsafe.” Life evolved amid constant natural radiation — every second, thousands of natural particles pass through you harmlessly. Risk depends on dose, and small doses carry vanishingly small risk.

rows.definition: Radioactive material that has been deposited on materials, skin, clothing or any place where it is not wanted, or that has been breathed in, swallowed or absorbed through a wound. A person is externally contaminated if the material is on the skin or clothing, and internally contaminated if it is inside the body. The environment is contaminated if radioactive material is spread about or is unconfined. If radioactive material is not in a sealed source container, it might be spread onto other objects.
quick_facts: Contamination is radioactive material on or in something
Radiation itself does not spread; the material does
Can be on skin or clothes, breathed in or swallowed, or spread about a place
A contaminated person is exposed until the material is removed
Material on skin or clothes can often be washed off
rows.debunking_snippet: “Radiation spreads onto people.” Radiation does not get on or in people. It is radioactive contamination, the material itself, that can be spread.

rows.definition: Leftover materials carrying radioactive contamination or activation, sorted into classes by activity and lifetime: very-low-level (soil, rubble), low-level (gloves, filters — most of the volume), intermediate (reactor components), and high-level (spent fuel and reprocessing residues — most of the radioactivity, in a tiny package). High-level waste is hot and long-lived, managed by decades of on-site cooling followed by either deep geological disposal or recycling, since roughly 95% of spent fuel's potential energy remains unused.
quick_facts: Four classes: VLLW → LLW → ILW → HLW
Volume is remarkably small — a country's lifetime HLW fits one facility
~95% of spent fuel's energy is still unused
Finland built the world's first permanent deep repository (Onkalo)
Managed under IAEA cradle-to-grave rules worldwide
rows.debunking_snippet: “Nuclear waste stays lethal for millions of years.” The intensely radioactive isotopes burn out fastest — within centuries waste converges toward the radioactivity of the original uranium ore it came from.

rows.definition: What happens when an unstable nucleus changes into a steadier one and gives off radiation. It happens by itself, and heating a material or changing it chemically hardly affects it. Radioactivity is natural: it is found in rocks, in the air, in food, in space and in your own body. Henri Becquerel discovered it in 1896 in a uranium mineral.
quick_facts: It comes from an unstable nucleus
It happens on its own, without anyone starting it
Natural sources: rocks, air, food, space and the human body
Henri Becquerel discovered it in 1896
People can make radioactive atoms, but most radioactivity is natural
rows.debunking_snippet: “Radioactivity is something humans created.” It is as old as the Earth. People only learned to find it, measure it and use it.

rows.definition: An unstable isotope — a radioactive nuclide — that sheds excess energy by decaying until it reaches stability. Some are primordial leftovers from before Earth formed (uranium-238), some are continuously created by cosmic rays (carbon-14), and hundreds are manufactured in reactors and cyclotrons. Medicine leans on them heavily: technetium-99m lights up ~30 million diagnostic scans a year, iodine-131 treats thyroid disorders, cobalt-60 sterilizes equipment.
quick_facts: Unstable nucleus → decays toward stability
Natural ones: U-238, C-14, K-40 · Man-made: Tc-99m, Co-60
Tc-99m: ~30 million medical scans yearly
Each carries a unique, unchangeable half-life signature
Identified by emitted energies like a fingerprint

rows.definition: A colorless, odorless radioactive gas seeping from trace uranium in soil, rock, and building materials — the heaviest gas and a noble one, so it drifts freely into basements and lower floors. Its short-lived daughter products stick in lungs and emit alpha particles there, making radon the leading cause of lung cancer among non-smokers and the single largest natural dose for most people. Cheap test kits and sub-slab ventilation fix problem buildings.
quick_facts: Noble gas from uranium decay in the ground
#2 cause of lung cancer overall, #1 among non-smokers
Pool in basements — heavier than air
WHO action reference: ~300 Bq/m³ indoors
Fixed cheaply with sub-slab depressurization vents
rows.debunking_snippet: “Radon is only a problem in uranium mines.” It's everywhere — the average home holds some, and tightly sealed modern houses can concentrate it. Testing costs less than a pizza.

rows.definition: The heart of the reactor: a carefully engineered lattice of fuel assemblies, moderator, coolant channels, and control elements where the chain reaction lives. Geometry is everything — spacing determines how neutrons bounce between fuel and moderator, keeping the reaction exactly critical. Cores hold tonnes of ceramic fuel at hundreds of degrees, transfer megawatts of heat to the coolant, and shut themselves down when control rods drop in. Everything else in the plant exists to serve or protect it.
quick_facts: Lattice of fuel assemblies + moderator + control rods
Runs at exactly k = 1 — self-sustaining but steady
Ceramic pellets reach service temperatures >500 °C
Refueled in thirds every 12–24 months
Wrapped in pressure vessel, shielding, containment

rows.definition: A legacy unit measuring radiation exposure — strictly, the ionization produced in dry air by X-rays or gamma rays: 1 R equals 2.58×10⁻⁴ coulombs of charge per kilogram of air. Named after Wilhelm Röntgen, discoverer of X-rays and winner of the first Nobel Prize in Physics (1901). It measures what radiation does to air, not to tissue, and has been superseded — though it lingers in old instruments, film badges, and disaster folklore.
quick_facts: Measures ionization in air, not dose to people
1 R = 2.58×10⁻⁴ C/kg of air
Honors Wilhelm Röntgen, first Physics Nobel (1901)
Roughly comparable to a rem for early gamma exposures
Still seen on vintage meters and in Chernobyl accounts
rows.debunking_snippet: “Roentgens and sieverts are interchangeable.” They measure different things: R counts ionization in air; sieverts weigh biological effect on tissue. Old meters read R — converting needs care and context.

rows.definition: A radiation detector that turns invisible energy into visible light: incoming radiation makes a scintillator crystal or plastic flash, and a photomultiplier tube amplifies each flicker into a measurable electrical pulse. Unlike Geiger counters, which only count events, the pulse height carries the particle's energy — letting scintillators identify exactly which isotope they're looking at from its spectral fingerprint. They power airport portal monitors, PET scanners, and physics discoveries from neutrino telescopes to dark-matter searches.
quick_facts: Radiation in → light flash → amplified pulse
Measures energy, not just counts — identifies isotopes
NaI(Tl) crystals and plastics are classic scintillators
Inside every PET scanner
Used to sniff out smuggled nuclear material at borders
rows.debunking_snippet: “All radiation detectors are basically Geiger counters.” Geiger-Müller tubes count clicks but stay blind to energy — scintillators read spectra and can name the isotope standing in front of them.

rows.definition: Material placed between you and a radiation source to cut intensity. Each radiation type needs its own answer: alphas stop in paper or skin, betas in a few millimeters of plastic, gamma rays are only ever attenuated — halved by each layer of dense lead or concrete — while fast neutrons need hydrogen-rich material like water or polyethylene to slow down, plus boron to capture them. Pick the wrong shield and it can backfire: lead around betas manufactures X-rays.
quick_facts: Alpha: paper · Beta: plastic · Gamma: dense metal/concrete
Gammas are attenuated, never fully blocked
Neutrons want hydrogen-rich shields + boron capture
Time–distance–shielding: three levers, one goal
Wrong shield (lead on betas) creates secondary X-rays
rows.debunking_snippet: “Lead stops everything.” Lead is useless against alpha (paper beats it), can worsen beta fields via secondary X-rays, and merely thins gamma beams — shielding is matched to the radiation, not bought off the shelf.

rows.definition: The SI unit of dose in terms of biological effect, named after Swedish radiological-health pioneer Rolf Sievert. It starts from absorbed dose (grays) and applies two weightings: radiation type (alphas count 20× harder than gammas) and tissue sensitivity. Context makes it tangible: a transatlantic flight adds ~40 μSv, a chest X-ray ~0.1 mSv, a CT scan ~7 mSv, against ~2.4 mSv of natural background per year.
quick_facts: Weighted for biology: gray × radiation factor × tissue factor
Alphas weighted 20× more damaging than gammas per gray
Flight NYC→London: ~40 μSv · CT scan: ~7 mSv
Natural background: ~2.4 mSv/year average
Occupational limit: 20 mSv/year averaged over five years
rows.debunking_snippet: “A sievert of any radiation feels the same.” The whole point of sieverts is that it doesn't — the same absorbed gray becomes twenty times riskier when it comes from alpha emitters inside your lungs.

rows.definition: Fuel assemblies removed from a reactor after roughly 4–6 years, when fission products build up and efficiency drops. Far from empty, an assembly still holds about 93% uranium-238, ~1% plutonium, and ~5% split fragments — leaving most of its original energy unburned. Fresh out of the core it's fiercely radioactive and heat-generating, so it spends at least five years underwater, then decades in ventilated dry casks while nations debate deep repositories or recycling.
quick_facts: Composition: ~93% uranium · ~5% fission products · ~1% plutonium
Water pools first (≥5 years), then sealed dry casks
Casks survive crashes, fires, and floods by design
~95% of its possible energy is still unused — recycling exists
Finland's Onkalo is the first permanent deep repository

sources.title: Storage and Disposal of Spent Nuclear Fuel

rows.debunking_snippet: “Spent fuel is useless garbage.” It's mostly untouched uranium plus freshly made plutonium — countries like France reprocess it into new fuel rods rather than burying it.

rows.definition: Polish-American mathematician (1909–1984) who cracked the hydrogen bomb's central problem. In 1951 he proposed using radiation from a fission explosion itself to compress and ignite fusion fuel — the 'radiation implosion' insight that became the Teller–Ulam design behind every thermonuclear weapon since. A Manhattan Project veteran, he also co-invented the Monte Carlo method with John von Neumann over playing cards, pioneered early computing applications, and sketched nuclear-pulse propulsion for Project Orion.
quick_facts: Idea man behind the Teller–Ulam H-bomb design (1951)
Co-invented the Monte Carlo method with von Neumann
Manhattan Project mathematician at Los Alamos
Designed Project Orion's nuclear-pulse propulsion concept
Survived leukemia thanks to one of the first chemotherapy successes
rows.debunking_snippet: “Teller alone invented the hydrogen bomb.” The breakthrough — compressing fusion fuel with X-rays from a fission trigger — came from Ulam's calculations; Teller ran with it. Both names belong on the design.

rows.definition: The force that holds the protons and neutrons together inside a nucleus. It is much stronger than the electric push between protons, but it only works over a very short distance, about the size of a nucleus. In a stable nucleus the strong force wins over the push. If the balance is wrong, the nucleus is unstable.
quick_facts: It holds the nucleus together
It is much stronger than the electric push between protons
It only works over about the size of a nucleus
Neutrons feel it too, but they have no charge, so they do not push
It is one of the four basic forces of nature

sources.title: University Physics Volume 3: Nuclear Binding Energy

rows.debunking_snippet: “Neutrons are just glue.” Neutrons feel the strong force and have no charge, so they change the balance in a nucleus. But the balance depends on the whole mix of protons and neutrons, not on neutrons alone.

rows.definition: A neutron slowed to thermal equilibrium with its surroundings — about 0.025 eV of energy and a leisurely 2.2 km/s, versus a newborn fission neutron's 20,000 km/s. The slowdown matters enormously: uranium-235's capture cross-section balloons from about 1 barn at high speed to roughly 585 barns at thermal energies, which is why almost every power reactor carries a moderator to provide them. Uranium-238, meanwhile, prefers to swallow faster neutrons — the reason moderation and enrichment go hand in hand.
quick_facts: ≈0.025 eV · ≈2.2 km/s — room temperature equilibrium
U-235 fission cross-section: ~585 barns thermal vs ~1 barn fast
Produced by bouncing fast neutrons off light nuclei
The design target of every moderated reactor
Cadmium and boron absorb them voraciously

rows.definition: Changing one element into another by altering the number of protons in its nucleus — through radioactive decay or deliberate bombardment. Rutherford achieved the first artificial transmutation in 1919 (nitrogen into oxygen), fulfilling the alchemists' dream by physics rather than philosophy. Every element heavier than iron was forged by transmutation inside stars or supernovae, reactors breed plutonium from uranium-238 by it, and proposed 'partitioning and transmutation' schemes would blast long-lived waste isotopes into shorter-lived ones.
quick_facts: Alchemy's goal, achieved via nuclear physics (Rutherford, 1919)
Decay chains are nature's own slow transmutation
Elements beyond iron were born in stars and supernovae
Reactors transmute U-238 into plutonium-239 routinely
Proposed as a way to shrink long-lived nuclear waste
rows.debunking_snippet: “Chemistry can change one element into another.” No chemical process can — chemistry only rearranges electrons. Changing elements requires changing the nucleus itself.

rows.definition: Hydrogen with two neutrons added (³H) — radioactive, with a 12.3-year half-life and a feeble beta particle that a sheet of paper stops. Nature makes only traces in the upper atmosphere, so commercial supplies come from heavy-water reactors and weapons programs. It's the fuel partner for deuterium in fusion experiments, boosts the yield of thermonuclear weapons, keeps watch dials glowing for decades, and serves as a biology tracer.
quick_facts: Hydrogen +2 neutrons · half-life 12.3 years
Weakest common beta emitter (~5.7 keV average)
D–T is fusion's easiest reaction — ITER runs on it
Boosts thermonuclear weapon yields
Glows in exit signs and watch faces via phosphor excitation
rows.debunking_snippet: “Those glowing exit signs are radiation hazards.” Tritium's betas cannot escape the sealed glass tube — stand as close as you like for as long as you like; distance of millimeters protects you completely.

rows.definition: The fissile star of natural uranium — just 0.72% of the metal, yet the only isotope found in nature that sustains chain reactions easily. Its nucleus deforms and splits when it captures a slow neutron, releasing ~200 MeV plus fresh neutrons. With a 704-million-year half-life it still accounts for nearly all of Earth's remaining U-235; the Oklo deposit in Gabon burned some naturally two billion years ago when concentrations ran higher.
quick_facts: 0.72% of natural uranium
Fissile with slow (thermal) neutrons
~200 MeV per split · 2–3 neutrons out
Half-life: 704 million years
Gabon's Oklo went critical naturally ~1.7 billion years ago

rows.definition: Ninety-nine point three percent of natural uranium and the quiet majority of every fuel rod. It won't sustain chain reactions itself — thermal neutrons bounce off it — but fast neutrons occasionally split it, and captured neutrons transform it into plutonium-239 inside any running reactor. Its 4.47-billion-year half-life sets Earth's uranium clock, and its depleted form (left over after enrichment) balances tanks and shields gamma rays.
quick_facts: 99.28% of natural uranium · half-life 4.47 billion years
Fertile: becomes fissile Pu-239 after capturing a neutron
Fast neutrons can split it — adding extra energy in reactors
Depleted uranium: tank armor and radiation shielding
Dating rocks by U-238 → lead-206 decay chains

rows.definition: One uranium atom bonded to six fluorines — the compound that makes enrichment practical. It sublimes directly from solid to gas at just 56 °C under normal pressure, letting centrifuge cascades work on a gas whose molecules differ only by the whisper of mass between U-235 and U-238. The trade-off: UF₆ is ferociously reactive with moisture, breaking down into corrosive hydrofluoric acid, so it travels in rugged cylinders under strict handling rules.
quick_facts: Sublimes at 56 °C — the working gas of enrichment
Only volatile uranium compound suitable for centrifuges
Reacts violently with water → hydrofluoric acid
Shipped internationally in thick-walled steel cylinders
Fluorine comes back out unchanged — reused endlessly

rows.definition: Locking high-level liquid waste inside glass — literally. Waste is calcined into powder, melted together with borosilicate glass formers at over 1,000 °C, and poured into stainless steel canisters where it solidifies into chemically inert logs. Glass resists leaching for many thousands of years, packs the waste densely, and tolerates radiation damage gracefully. France has run industrial-scale vitrification at La Hague since 1978; Hanford's massive treatment plant is finally doing the same for America's Cold War tank waste.
quick_facts: Waste dissolved into borosilicate glass at >1,000 °C
Glass logs resist leaching across geological timescales
France (La Hague) vitrifying industrially since 1978
Hanford's plant addresses Cold War-era tank waste
Canisters designed to cool for decades before disposal
rows.debunking_snippet: “Waste is stored in leaky barrels.” High-level liquid waste is the dangerous legacy — and vitrification turns it into solid glass that geologists expect to outlast human civilization.

rows.definition: The SI unit of power — one joule per second — named for Scottish engineer James Watt, whose steam engines powered the first industrial revolution. Nuclear plants are rated two ways that matter: thermal megawatts describe heat from the core (a typical large unit: ~3,000 MWt), while electrical megawatts describe what reaches the grid (~1,000 MWe) — the gap being thermodynamic efficiency. A single large reactor thus powers around a million homes continuously, day and night.
quick_facts: 1 W = 1 joule per second
Named after James Watt (honored 1889, formalized in SI)
Plants quote MWt (heat) and MWe (electricity)
Typical large unit: ~3,000 MWt → ~1,000 MWe
~33% efficiency set by steam-cycle thermodynamics

rows.definition: Electromagnetic radiation born when fast electrons slam into matter — decelerating violently (bremsstrahlung) or knocking inner-shell electrons loose. Wilhelm Röntgen discovered them accidentally in 1895 and photographed his wife's hand within weeks, launching medical imaging and winning the first Nobel Prize in Physics (1901). Energies overlap with gamma rays; the difference is origin — X-rays come from electron processes, gammas from nuclei. Hospitals fire LINAC-built beams through patients millions of times daily.
quick_facts: Discovered by Röntgen (1895) — first Nobel in Physics
Born from electron interactions, unlike nuclear gamma rays
Softer than most gammas but the ranges overlap
CT scans stack hundreds of X-ray slices
Lead aprons attenuate scattered rays during imaging
rows.debunking_snippet: “X-rays make you radioactive afterward.” Impossible — X-rays pass through and vanish at light speed. Only neutron bombardment activates materials, and hospital X-rays aren't neutrons.

rows.definition: Milled, concentrated uranium oxide — mostly U₃O₈ — named for its buttery color though modern versions run khaki to black. It's the checkpoint between mine and fuel cycle: leached from ore, precipitated, dried, packed into drums worth tens of thousands of dollars each. Chemically stable and only weakly radioactive, yellowcake still contains mostly uranium-238 — far from anything fissile until conversion and enrichment transform it.
quick_facts: Mostly U₃O₈ — 70–90% uranium by weight
Color varies: yellow, khaki, brown, black
Weakly radioactive — alpha emitters, handled with gloves
Each drum holds roughly a tonne of uranium value
Cannot detonate or power anything without conversion + enrichment
rows.debunking_snippet: “Yellowcake is a step toward building bombs.” As sold, it's overwhelmingly non-fissile U-238 — unusable in weapons without the entire industrial apparatus of conversion and enrichment on top.

rows.definition: The explosive energy of a nuclear weapon, quoted in tons or megatons of TNT equivalent (1 kiloton = 4.184 trillion joules). Hiroshima's Little Boy delivered about 15 kilotons from a single fission stage; modern thermonuclear warheads reach hundreds of kilotons to megatons by wrapping a fission trigger around fusion fuel. Yield splits between blast, thermal pulse, prompt radiation, and fallout — whose severity depends on burst height and design choices.
quick_facts: Measured in TNT equivalents: kt, Mt
Hiroshima: ~15 kt · largest ever tested: 50 Mt (Tsar Bomba)
Fission primary ignites the fusion secondary in modern weapons
Airbursts maximize blast; ground bursts maximize fallout
1 kt = 4.184 × 10¹² joules

rows.definition: Shorthand for atomic number — Z stands for the German 'Zahl' (number), dating to pre-WWI physics papers written in German. Physically it counts protons and thereby fixes an atom's place in the periodic table: hydrogen Z = 1, carbon Z = 6, uranium Z = 92. In nuclear formulas Z tracks charge balance through reactions — sum the Z's before and after any decay or collision and the totals must match.
quick_facts: Z = German 'Zahl', meaning number
Counts protons — fixes the element
Conserved across every nuclear reaction

rows.definition: A research reactor deliberately run at microscopic power — watts to microwatts, sometimes dubbed 'zero-power'. At those levels the core barely warms, so no cooling systems, big shielding, or containment dome are required; universities and labs use them to teach reactor physics hands-on, test lattice configurations, and measure criticality safely. Students can pull rods themselves and watch reactivity respond in real time — impossible at full power.
quick_facts: Operates at watts to microwatts — effectively zero power
No meaningful heat → minimal cooling or shielding needed
Used for teaching, lattice tests, and criticality measurements
Students operate controls directly under supervision
Proves designs before full-power construction begins
rows.debunking_snippet: “All reactors are industrial monsters.” Zero-power reactors fit in gymnasiums, hum along at flashlight-battery heating levels, and have trained generations of nuclear engineers safely.
